## v3.66.760 - MOD-1 A-5b: takeover idle-timeout + the A5-R3 no-orphan sweep
- New captcha_takeover_idle_timeout_s (default 300): a remote solve session with no operator
  input for this long is finalized (dismissed + ender + channel closed). The clock resets on
  each accepted input; the SSE viewer stream honors the same bound and a viewer disconnect
  tears the channel down, freeing the A-5a concurrency slot (a reconnect re-opens it).
- captcha_relay.sweep_report: the A5-R3 project-canonical no-orphan sweep. ONE atomic registry
  (_pending under _lock) is the source of truth; the sweep DERIVES its active set from it and
  CROSS-CHECKS the live surfaces against that set - every open takeover channel (not just the
  ones the registry remembers) and every live solve browser via a census hook. A live surface
  the registry does not bind is an orphan and is reaped. A surface the sweep CANNOT verify
  (census unregistered or raising) is reported in `unverified` - unknown-fails-to-reap, never a
  silent "0 orphans". sweep_expired keeps its legacy int contract (count of tracked sessions
  swept) and delegates to sweep_report.
- The reaper now actually runs: captcha_relay.start_sweeper (daemon, BD_DISABLE_KEEPALIVE-
  guarded), wired in app.py alongside a live-browser session census. Previously sweep_expired
  had zero production callers - a reaper nobody runs protects nothing.
- takeover.list_channel_sids exposes the full channel denominator for the sweep's cross-check.
- CONFIG-KEY-ADD footgun applied in the same cut: idle-timeout key FE-wired (api-types +
  settingsSchema + Settings.tsx control) + two config_gui_manifest rows (the config key and its
  BD_CAPTCHA_TAKEOVER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_S env-seed alias); no new import edge (baseline holds 1333).

## v3.66.759 - MOD-1 A-5a: remote-takeover admission controls (kill-switch + concurrency cap)
- New captcha_takeover_enabled (bool, SAFETY-BEARING, fail-closed to OFF): the master kill-switch
  for remote takeover. Remote (headless + screencast) engages only when mode=remote AND this is
  enabled AND under the concurrency cap; any gate failing falls back to visible (a solve is never
  blocked, only kept off the remote path). Flip off to instantly stop all remote takeover.
- New captcha_takeover_max_concurrent (default 2): caps simultaneous remote solve sessions
  (open takeover channels); beyond it, new solves fall back to visible.
- runner_auth admission helpers (_takeover_enabled, _takeover_max_concurrent, _remote_admitted);

## v3.66.754 - the ledger's auditor and the parity scanner could not see their own subjects

Two cuts, one shape: a check whose denominator structurally excludes the thing it is
asked about reports clean -- truthfully, and uselessly.

754a -- decided_against was a WRITE-ONLY section of the task tracker.
  * tasktracker_gen hardcoded sections=[incomplete, awaiting_operator, completed]. The
    fourth declared section was neither AUDITED nor RENDERED nor COUNTED: 16 rows of
    decisions existed only in the JSON. Injecting a row conforming to NO schema returned
    "[OK] schema conforms | RESULT: CLEAN". The thumbs/a11y closure REASONS -- the record
    of why an arbitrary-file-read surface must not be wired -- were filed into a section
    no reader ever sees.
  * FIXED BY DERIVING, not by adding a fourth branch: consumers now read a SECTION_SCHEMAS
    registry, and an UNRECOGNISED section is a LOUD failure, not a silent skip. The next
    section added cannot be invisible by default.
  * FOUND WHILE FIXING IT -- a FOURTH consumer nobody had counted. tasktracker_sync (the
    in-sync gate that build_session_pack.py:114 HARD-GATES the pack build on) carried the
    same hardcoded list THREE more times: it read 2 of 5 sheets, recognised 2 of 4 md
    headings, and compared 2 of 4 buckets. On the shipped tracker md saw 38/374 while xlsx
    saw 12/359 -- the gate was comparing two DIFFERENTLY-WRONG numbers. Session close was
    already broken. One registry now feeds all three.
  * AND THE DRIFT THAT WAS HIDING BEHIND IT: with the denominator fixed, a real drift
    surfaced immediately -- IDEA-HARDEN was in the xlsx and not the md. The md header-skip
    was `not ln.startswith("| ID")`, a PREFIX match, so the legitimate row `| IDEA-HARDEN |`
    was mistaken for the header and dropped. It survived because BOTH sides were wrong and
    the errors cancelled. A gate with two wrong sides can pass a real drift.
  * precut_check mapped tasktracker_gen.py to ONE test, so editing the tool did not band
    its own audit gate. A band map is a denominator too.

754b -- gui_parity was WIRED BY PROSE, and BLIND TO CODE.
  * _spa_wiring harvested /api/ literals from RAW TEXT, so a path merely NAMED in a comment
    counted as a call site. Comments are now stripped first -- with a STATE MACHINE, not a
    regex: a naive strip treats a `/*` inside a `//` comment as a block opener, and one such
    line in Dedup.tsx ate 6,448 chars of live code and fabricated 22 "phantoms" that
    included REAL, CALLED endpoints. That incident is now a regression pin.
  * THE STRIP COULD NOT SHIP ALONE. Six of the eight endpoints it un-wires are REAL,
    OPERABLE controls the CALL HARVEST could not see -- the comment was MASKING two harvest
    defects, not reporting dark controls. Both fixed in the same cut:
      - _norm_ep stripped the query BEFORE collapsing ${...}, so a JS nullish `??` inside a
        template expression was eaten as a query delimiter and the path was DISCARDED. The
        harvest was fine; the NORMALISER was the bug. (widgets GET/PUT/DELETE)
      - _resolve_dynamic_dispatchers already existed for exactly this case but required a
        BARE identifier; Vpn.tsx dispatches through the MEMBER EXPRESSION ${t.action}, so
        the resolver never even recognised it. (vpn tunnels start/stop/cycle)
  * BLAST RADIUS, DERIVED AND VERIFIED BY CONTENT DIFF (never by the count): spa_wired
    426 -> 424. Un-wired: GET /api/dev/auth_map, POST /api/playground/test. Newly wired:
    none. Both phantoms FALSIFIED BY GREP before being accepted: each has exactly ONE
    occurrence in the SPA and both are comments. /api/playground/test's is a comment that
    DENIES the call -- the denial wired it.
  * spa_wiring_unresolved: indirected call sites (apiGet(url)) are now REPORTED as an
    explicit third state. A scanner that cannot read a call site must say so, or unknown is
    silently folded into ABSENT.

## v3.66.748 - CSRF column DERIVED from the hook (audit R11-13); .hypothesis forbidden (R18)

The two remaining round-2 audit findings. R11-13 was its highest-severity item,
and the fix it asked for is a test, not a patch.

THE DRIFT. _check_csrf gates ("/api/", "/cockpit/api/"). The scanner every
artifact calls (build_endpoint_catalog._csrf_fires_for) had RE-TYPED that rule
and never learned the second prefix, so 28 cockpit write endpoints were
PROTECTED by the app and reported csrf:false by ROUTE_INDEX, ENDPOINT_CATALOG,
and -- the one that SHIPS -- the OpenAPI spec at /api/openapi.json, which
therefore omitted the required X-CSRF-Token header and the 403 response for
them. A generated client breaks on its first cockpit write; a reviewer reads
the spec and concludes cockpit is unprotected. It is not.

THE PART THAT MATTERS MOST (R13): because the artifact already said false,
someone dropping /cockpit/api/ from the hook would change NO artifact and trip
NO gate. The mirror being wrong in the SAFE direction had burned down the alarm
for a move in the DANGEROUS one.

DON'T MIRROR -- DERIVE:
- app.py now exports the route-level CSRF policy as the single source of truth:
  CSRF_TRIPPING_METHODS, CSRF_GUARDED_PREFIXES, CSRF_EXEMPT_PATHS, and the one
  predicate csrf_fires_for(). _check_csrf READS them (the prefix tuple and the
  pair/redeem exemption are no longer inlined -- there is nothing left to copy).
- build_endpoint_catalog binds to the APP'S OBJECTS (lazily: a module-scope
  import would beat _import_app's BD_DISABLE_KEEPALIVE=1 and spawn the very
  subsystems that tool exists to keep asleep) and _csrf_fires_for DELEGATES to
  the app's predicate.
- Artifacts regenerated: ROUTE_INDEX (28 csrf flips, all cockpit, all
  false->true -- matching the audit's count exactly), ENDPOINT_CATALOG, and
  openapi.json (28 cockpit write ops now declare X-CSRF-Token + a 403).
- New gate: tests/test_v3_66_748_csrf_scanner_derives_from_hook.py. Proves the
  derivation TWO ways: structurally (the scanner's constants ARE the app's
  objects -- identity, not equality, so a fork cannot even be expressed) and
  BEHAVIOURALLY (for every mutating route on the live app, drive the REAL hook
  with a cookie session and no token and compare the actual 403 to the
  scanner's verdict). The behavioural half is the alarm R13 asked for: it fails
  the day the hook and the scanner disagree. Plus a can-it-fail control.
  NO app behaviour change -- the app was always right.

R18 -- .hypothesis/ (and the audit's one wrong assumption):
- 27 .hypothesis/ entries were SHIPPING while the forbidden-artifact gate
  reported clean: its denominator did not contain them (0 of 27 flagged). The
  signature failure of this program, once more.
- FIXED at both ends: .hypothesis excluded from the release manifest
  (dev_suite._MANIFEST_EXCLUDE_DIRS -> keeps it OUT of the build) and added to
  diff_release_zips.FORBIDDEN_SEGMENT (-> if it ever returns, the gate SAYS so
  instead of reporting clean over it).
- The audit said this needed a guard-SHA re-declaration because build_release.py
  is guard #7. It did NOT: the forbidden lists live in diff_release_zips.py and
  the exclusion set in dev_suite/release_lint.py, neither of which is
  guard-pinned. Verified against bd-guardcheck's 7-file list BEFORE editing.
  All 7 guard SHAs remain byte-identical.

## v3.66.747 - exec-bridge option-injection guards (audit round 2, R14)

tool_bridge is a strong control (no shell, resolved argv0, path containment,
minimal env, 30s timeout, 256KiB cap) with one gap the round-2 audit found: a
POSITIONAL whose value looks like an option passed straight to the tool, because
build_argv appended positionals with no `--` separator and the url str-positional
had no leading-dash / scheme guard. build_argv("yt-dlp", {"url": "--evil"}) ->
['yt-dlp', '--evil']. Not shell injection (the no-shell defense holds) -- OPTION
injection into the tool itself (yt-dlp options can write files, run
post-processors, read option files). CSRF-gated + same-origin, so
defense-in-depth, not a remote hole -- but the bridge's whole premise is
"paranoid, centrally."

Three guards, belt-and-suspenders:
- build_argv now inserts a `--` end-of-options separator before positionals
  (only when there are any). Everything after `--` is a positional operand the
  tool cannot parse as an option.
- str positional values that begin with '-' are REFUSED at validation (400),
  not merely fenced.
- The url positional gained an opt-in scheme allowlist (["http","https"]),
  mirroring the rigor the `path` type already has: file://, ftp://, javascript:
  and non-URL values are refused.

New gate: tests/test_v3_66_747_exec_bridge_option_injection.py -- the case the
717 suite lacked (its denominator was "unknown flag KEYS"; the gap was "known
positional VALUES"). RED-first: 4/4 failing on 746 source. The existing 717 +
719 + 730 bridge suites stay green (the `--` separator does not disturb the

## v3.66.746 - L34 gates the operator surface; diagnostics are advisory

The 745 stash capture proved L34 finally WORKS -- 8 workers + triage + serial
re-confirmation probed 423 routes and correctly surfaced /api/dev/bat_lint as
a real >8s route -- and it still FAILed the deploy, for the program's oldest
reason: the wrong denominator. Of 122s total sweep cost, 79s (65%) was the
/api/dev + /cockpit/api DIAGNOSTIC surface: 202 routes, 28 of 41 slow ones.
bat_lint, lockfile_scan, sh_lint, secret_scan, mem_audit are INTROSPECTION
endpoints that do real scan work by design. Failing an operator deploy because
a dev tool's filesystem walk takes 9s asserts the wrong thing at the wrong cost.

L34's own docstring calls it "the natural post-deploy gate" -- for the OPERATOR
surface. So partition it:

- OPERATOR routes (not /api/dev, not /cockpit) are the HARD GATE: a 5xx or
  unreachable there FAILs, exactly as before. In-sandbox that is 265 of 524
  param-free GET routes; on the capture ~220 routes at ~196ms = ~43s of work,
  which fits phase 1 at 8 workers with no UNPROBED.
- DIAGNOSTIC routes are still SMOKED -- in a labeled ADVISORY pass on leftover
  wall, at the triage budget, that REPORTS slow/5xx/unreachable dev routes
  (named, counted, in both log and verdict tail) but does NOT fail the deploy.
  Dropping them would be the "shrink the denominator to hide a finding" sin
  this program exists to prevent; reporting-but-not-gating is the honest scope.

The advisory pass never eats the operator gate's wall (it runs only after, only
with _left() budget) and never blocks on a hung dev route (short per-probe
timeout). bat_lint stays visible -- it is a real slow route -- it just no longer
sinks the operator deploy gate.

- New gate: tests/test_v3_66_746_l34_operator_gate.py -- a clean operator
  surface behind a wall of hanging diagnostics PASSES while still naming them
  (RED-first); an operator 5xx still FAILs; no operator UNPROBED.
- tests/test_v3_66_737: the "genuinely slow route still FAILs" case moved to an
  operator route (its old /cockpit route is now correctly advisory), with a
  companion pinning the diagnostic case as advisory-but-visible.

FOLLOW-UP (product, not harness): bat_lint and lockfile_scan/sh_lint are
genuinely slow filesystem walks. 742 pruned bat_lint's walk denominator; the
same prune likely applies to lockfile_scan/sh_lint/secret_scan. Tracked for a
product cut -- now surfaced as advisory findings instead of a deploy-blocker.

## v3.66.745 - L34 workers 4 -> 8 (reverses my 741 decision, on stash evidence)

The 744 stash capture: triage fixed the slow-route starvation AND the sweep
still missed its deadline -- 346/523 UNPROBED. The log's own numbers close
the case: 157 probed routes sum to 66s of real latency (mean 420ms on a
loaded box; sibling live checks hammer the app during the sweep), 66/4
workers = 16.5s, plus 20 triage timeouts x 5s / 4 = 25s -- ~43s against the
39.6s phase-1 share. Meanwhile ALL 20 suspects RECOVERED serially in ~14s
(including /api/dev/bat_lint at 4.1s -- the 742 prune verified on stash; the
733 "five 8s routes" were contention ghosts).

So the constraint has moved: with triage (744) capping a suspect's phase-1
cost at 5s and serial re-confirmation clearing healthy routes at their real
latency, contention artifacts are CHEAP -- and throughput is not. The 741
workers cut treated the artifact symptom at the cost of the sweep. Workers
go back to 8: 66s of work is 8.3s at 8 workers; expected phase 1 ~25-30s
including contention-suspect timeouts, well inside the share, with the
reserve intact for recoveries.

- tests/test_v3_66_741_l34_phase1_bounded.py: workers pin updated 4 -> 8
  with the reversal rationale (a pin that moves must say why, with a capture).
- tests/test_v3_66_744_l34_triage_budget.py: NEW throughput control -- 64
  uniformly-moderate routes (0.25s) against the scaled phase-1 share fit at
  8 workers (2.0s) and starve at 4 (4.0s); proven RED on the 744 tree.
- The deadline + UNPROBED honesty remain the correctness floor: a
  pathological box still gets a truthful verdict, never an overrun.

## v3.66.744 - L34 phase 1 triages at a short budget (fixes the 743 regression I shipped)

THE 743 STASH CAPTURE: `[FAIL] L34 -- 372 route(s) UNPROBED (phase-1
deadline)`. The 741 deadline held (the honesty half worked) but the sweep
starved: phase 1 probed every route at the FULL 8s adjudication budget, so
each genuinely-slow route held one of the 4 workers for 8s -- one slow route
costs ~400 fast-route slots. 151 of 523 probed; 372 honestly UNPROBED. A
correct verdict about an incorrectly-budgeted sweep. My regression: 741
lowered the workers AND left phase 1 on the full budget; the sandbox test
missed it because its world was UNIFORMLY slow, a shape that cannot starve.

- NEW `_L34_TRIAGE_BUDGET_S = 5`: phase 1 probes at the short triage budget;
  a route that misses it is a SUSPECT, and phase 2 re-probes suspects
  serially at the full `_L34_ROUTE_BUDGET_S` inside the reserve. Triage
  decides who gets adjudicated; it never issues the verdict. 5s is above the
  heaviest healthy view measured alone (4.1s @733) so a slow-but-fine route
  is not manufactured into a suspect.
- Deadline + UNPROBED honesty unchanged -- they are the correctness property;
  triage is what makes throughput fit inside them. Stash arithmetic: ~40
  worker-seconds across 523 routes at 4 workers = ~10s of a 39.6s phase-1
  share, with the full reserve left for adjudication.
- Fixed the R15 audit finding while here: the _L34_WORKERS comment asserted
  "the wall clock tracks the SLOWEST route rather than the sum" -- only true
  when every probe is cheap; rewritten with the real cost model (K*B/W).
- New gate: tests/test_v3_66_744_l34_triage_budget.py, modeling the BIMODAL
  stash shape (12 hanging routes ahead of 60 fast ones; starvation is
  arithmetic, not scheduling luck). RED proven mechanically: the
  bd-mutation-test row L34/triage-starvation@744 re-plants the full budget in
  the phase-1 submit and the gate goes RED (CAUGHT 1/1). An earlier draft of
  the test produced a FALSE RED (its assertion matched the literal "0
  unprobed" summary token) -- caught by hand-verifying the mutation survivor,
  which is the reason that rule exists.

Root cause: `_repo_root().rglob(...)`. The release zip's tree is ~2.5k
files, but the lints run against the INSTALL DIR on stash -- which accretes
everything the zip never ships: the service venv, frontend node_modules,
__pycache__, and overlay orphans (the overlay never deletes). rglob walked
all of it to find a handful of scripts. The route was slow because its
denominator was the wrong tree.

  (`_LINT_WALK_EXCLUDE_DIRS is _MANIFEST_EXCLUDE_DIRS`, pinned by test).
- Deliberately NOT touched: zip_manifest_check keeps its full walk -- its
  job is spotting files that should not be there; pruning it would create a
  blind gate.
- Not just a speedup: a .bat inside venv/ is runtime accretion, not an

## v3.66.741 - L34 phase 1 honors the reserve it declared (workers 8 -> 4)

The 740 run's own number: 24 of 25 suspects UNCONFIRMED. The wall-aware fix
at 740 bounded phase 2 only -- `_L34_PHASE2_RESERVE = 0.45` was declared with
a comment ("fraction of the wall held back for re-confirmation") and NEVER
REFERENCED. Phase 1 ran an unbounded pool.map over every route; phase 2 got
the scraps. A reserve nobody enforces is a comment, not a budget.

- Phase 1 now runs under a deadline of `wall * (1 - reserve)`. At the
  deadline it cancels everything not-done in ONE sweep (a lazy per-iteration
  cancel races the pool's own queue-draining and never cancels anything --
  measured: the full 8s sweep ran to completion against a 1.5s wall). The
  <= workers in-flight probes drain within a single route budget, so the
  overshoot is bounded by one probe, never by the sweep.
- Routes phase 1 could not reach are UNPROBED -- named in the log, named in
  the verdict, and FAILING. Unknown is a third state; a deadline that
  silently shrank the denominator would be the blind-gate shape with a clock
  for a denominator. Every route lands in exactly one bucket:
  ok / confirmed / recovered / UNCONFIRMED / UNPROBED.
- `_L34_WORKERS` 8 -> 4. The 8-way fan-out manufactured the very suspects
  phase 2 then had no budget to clear (37 false suspects at 734, 25 at 740,
  nearly all contention artifacts; each costs a full serial probe budget to
  clear). Halving the fan-out roughly doubles phase-1 wall cost but starves
  phase 2 of artifacts -- which is where the budget actually went.
- New gate: tests/test_v3_66_741_l34_phase1_bounded.py (RED-first: 3 of 4
  proven failing on pristine 740 source; the fast-clean-app control passed
  throughout).

## v3.66.740 - L34 budgets itself against the harness wall (fixes the 737 regression)

- FIXES A BUG I SHIPPED AT 737, caught by the 737 capture: L34 TIMED OUT after 90s and
  leaked its thread AGAIN. 737 added serial re-confirmation (to strip the contention
  734's own 8-way fan-out was creating) and made it UNBOUNDED: ~37 suspects x 8s
  = ~300s against a 90s wall. The fix for the contamination reintroduced the timeout the
  contamination fix was built on top of. Two releases, same failure mode, opposite causes.
- THE REAL DEFECT, which neither 734 nor 737 addressed: L34 was never WALL-AWARE. The
  harness gives each check 90s and on expiry ABANDONS the thread -- which keeps smoking
  all 523 routes underneath L31 (memory) and L33 (leak scan) and poisons their readings.
  A check that CAN run past the wall does not merely fail, it corrupts the checks after
  it. Any check whose cost tracks a growing denominator (523 routes and climbing) will
  cross the wall eventually; bounding it is the correctness property, not an optimisation.
- L34 now watches the clock (_L34_WALL_S = 72s of the harness's 90s). Phase 2 re-confirms
  suspects only while budget remains. Whatever it cannot reach is UNCONFIRMED -- which is
  UNKNOWN, and unknown FAILS, named in the verdict. Never silently dropped, never assumed
  innocent. It cannot overrun, so it cannot leak the thread, so L31/L33 stop being
  measured underneath it.
- Mutation-tested: removing the wall check, and silently dropping unconfirmed suspects
  instead of failing on them, each turn tests red.

## v3.66.737 - L34: a concurrent probe must not report its OWN load as a finding

- FIXES A BUG I SHIPPED AT 734, caught by the 735 capture. 734 made L34 concurrent so
  it could finish 523 routes inside the harness's 90s wall. It finished -- and reported
  37 of 523 routes over the 8s budget. That number was CONTAMINATED.
- Measured serially in the 733 capture: /api/community_scrapers/index answers in 4090ms,
  /api/data/kb_analytics in 3613ms. Both appeared in 735's ">8s" list. A route that
  answers in 4.1s when probed ALONE is not an 8s route -- it doubled because an 8-way
  fan-out put load on the very app it was measuring. The instrument changed the thing it
  measured and reported its own contention back as a defect. That is the shape
  KB_JUDGMENT already names ("the fan-out WAS the slowdown; fan-out is a bet on cores you
  have") -- committed while fixing a different instance of it.
- FIX: phase 1 (concurrent) is TRIAGE and yields HYPOTHESES, not verdicts. Every non-ok
  route -- exceeded, 5xx, unreachable alike -- is RE-PROBED SERIALLY against a quiesced
  app. Only a route that STILL misbehaves alone is reported. One that recovers is logged
  RECOVERED ("phase-1 flag was our own load, not a defect") and is NOT a finding; a probe
  that quietly discards its own false positives teaches nobody anything.
- The verdict now says "did not answer within 8s WHEN PROBED ALONE", so a reader can tell
  a real finding from a contention artifact.
- Phase 2 only re-probes SUSPECTS (one extra GET each), so it does not cost the serial
  sweep it replaced. Concurrency buys the wall clock; it does not buy a verdict.
- Mutation-tested in BOTH directions: skipping phase 2 (the 734 bug) turns it red, and
  making phase 2 a laundry that passes everything ALSO turns it red.

## v3.66.736 - build_release._load_exclusions no longer poisons the interpreter (GUARD RE-SHA)

- GUARD SHA DECLARED: tools/build_release.py e8142436 -> f7c220d2 (operator-authorized).
- The @730 finding, fixed at the source. _load_exclusions() did
  `sys.path.insert(0, root)` + `from bulk_downloader.dev_suite import ...` and NEVER
  undid either. Run against a temp tree -- which is exactly what
  tools/precut_check.py::_tree_files does -- it left that tree on sys.path AND cached
  `bulk_downloader` -> the temp tree's STUB __init__ in sys.modules for the rest of the
  interpreter. Every later import of bulk_downloader then resolved to the stub.
- That is why version-pin / settings suites FAILED IN THE BAND but PASSED STANDALONE:
  the band shares one interpreter and whoever ran precut_check first poisoned it. A test
  that passes alone and fails in company is the tell.
- Now a try/finally pops the inserted path and restores sys.modules to exactly what it
  was -- evicting what this import caused, and re-binding anything it replaced. Safe for
  the two callables returned: _manifest_excluded is pure and zip_manifest_check only
  imports zipfile at call time; dropping a module from sys.modules does not destroy the
  module object while a function's __globals__ still references it.
- test_precut_check.py's snapshot/restore workaround stays as belt-and-braces, but it was
  a CALLER defending itself against a CALLEE that corrupted global state -- every future
  caller would have had to remember.
- Both halves mutation-tested: removing the path-pop and removing the sys.modules restore
  each turn exactly one test red.

## v3.66.734 - L34 full-route-smoke: EXCEEDED is a finding, not a story

- L34 FAILED on the 732 and 733 stash captures with "TIMEOUT after 90.0s -- thread
  leaked". The budget was fully accounted: 398 routes cost 7.5s (mean 19ms), 28 slow
  routes cost 42.3s, and FIVE routes cost 40.0s -- 44% of the wall -- by each burning
  the full 8s per-route timeout. It reached 426 of 523 routes.
- L34 logged each of those five as "TIMEOUT <rule> (likely a stream)" and returned
  WARN. That cause was ASSERTED, not observed, and it was wrong every time: all five
  are plain `return jsonify(...)` views (capture_diagnostics, replay_validation,
  housekeeping/preview, autonomy/queue, autonomy/notifications), and four are
  operator-facing (Report Center sections / cockpit views). The label hid an
  operator-facing performance defect for at least two releases.
- FIX: a route that blows its per-route budget is now EXCEEDED -- a third state that
  names NO cause and FAILS, naming the offending routes. A route that streams forever
  must be DECLARED in _L34_STREAMING_SKIP; an undeclared one that cannot answer is a
  defect or an undeclared stream, and only a human can say which. Unknown fails.
- FIX: the sweep is now concurrent (ThreadPoolExecutor, 8 workers; probes are
  I/O-bound and the app is threaded). 523 routes could not fit the harness's 90s wall
  serially and the route count only grows -- raising the ceiling is a treadmill. This
  also ends the thread leak, which had been smoking routes underneath L31/L33 and
  poisoning their readings (L31's "possible memory leak" is unproven as a result).
- The five slow routes are NOT added to the skip set -- that would delete the finding,
  and test_u44's test_skip_set_only_contains_streaming_routes already forbids it. A new
  test names all five so a future session cannot quietly silence them.
- All three new controls mutation-tested: restoring the "(likely a stream)" label,
  downgrading EXCEEDED to WARN, and reverting to a serial loop each turn exactly one
  test red.

## v3.66.732 - the 7 dark cockpit views get navigation: dark=0, orphans=0

The cockpit is ONE Flask route (/cockpit) rendering its views client-side: the
router dispatches PAGES[p](), so the renderable view set is the PAGES registry.
A view in PAGES with no <a data-p="..."> anchor and no REDIRECT alias is
UNREACHABLE -- fully implemented, renders fine, and no operator can ever get to
it. bd-gui-surface (rebuilt @729, after "44 views" turned out to be folklore)
derived SEVEN such views. None were stubs.

Wired, with anchors placed where each view belongs:
  Home     -- daily (Daily Mission), inbox (Inbox)
  Reports  -- orghealth (Org Health), maturity (Maturity), complexity (Complexity)
  Advanced -- advlanding (Advanced Overview), at the TOP of the drawer
  System   -- syslanding (System Overview), at the TOP of the drawer

advlanding and syslanding are the sharpest case in the set: their entire body is
nav cards pointing at other views. They are NAVIGATION HUBS THAT NOTHING
NAVIGATED TO. They now open their own drawers.

Surface: 133 renderable views, nav anchors 83 -> 90, 61 redirect aliases,
dark 7 -> 0, orphan anchors 0.

New suite tests/test_v3_66_732_cockpit_dark_views.py pins dark == 0 and orphans
== 0 GENERALLY -- not just for the seven -- so a future view added with no way in
fails the gate. It also guards the premise (the seven must remain REGISTERED:
deleting a view is not a way to make it reachable).

A NOTE ON THE TEST ITSELF: its first draft matched redirects as REDIRECTS['key']
lookups. The real source shape is a single object literal, const REDIRECT = {...},
so the pattern matched ZERO aliases and the test reported 50 dark views instead
of 7. The denominator was wrong, so the verdict was wrong -- the exact shape this
programme exists to catch, committed inside the test written to catch it. Caught
only because bd-gui-surface disagreed. Two independent derivations now converge
on 133/83/61/7, and the fixed test agrees with the tool exactly.

tools/cockpit_console.py only; no route change, no FE (SPA) change, no backend change.

v3.66.405 and NOTHING in the SPA could reach it. /api/webhooks (GET, POST),

## v3.66.729 -- the body-contract gate gets a WORLD (0 dead, UNKNOWN 83 -> 64)

726 built the body-contract gate and it was honest: it claimed DEAD only for what it
could prove, and reported the rest as UNKNOWN. But UNKNOWN was two-thirds of the
surface, and an endpoint we could not ask about is not an endpoint that passed.

It was blind for a reason it could not fix from where it stood: it replayed against an
EMPTY WORLD -- site id "_probe", task_id "x", a filename on no disk -- so endpoints
answered "unknown site_id" and the tool honestly said UNKNOWN. Its own docstring named
the fix: judging these needs REAL FIXTURES.

- ADD tools/body_contract_fixtures.py: a real world (a site, real `queue` rows, real
  library/tags/history rows, a real file on disk, ids of the RIGHT TYPE -- library ids
  are ints, and substituting a string 404s in ROUTING, not in the view).
- ADD tools/body_contract.probe_fixtures(): replays every typed call site into that
  world. OK 35 -> 53. UNKNOWN 83 -> 64. HARNESS-FAULT 4 -> 0. DEAD: 0.
- ADD tests/test_v3_66_729_body_contract_fixtures.py: DEAD == 0 and no 5xx are hard
  gates; UNKNOWN <= 64 is a ratchet that may only shrink.
- FOUND: ts_calls()/probe_typed() -- the whole type-directed differential probe, written
  and documented at 726 -- were never called by main(). Dead code. The "66 UNKNOWN"
  everyone quoted came from a capability nobody was running.

DEAD is 0. The 724/726 remediation held and nothing new has crept in. Getting to that
answer took 38 FALSE DEAD verdicts across five mechanisms, every one of them the
harness lying rather than the product breaking: a NO-BODY-ARG label that means "the
regex could not parse a literal" (apiPost's payload is a REQUIRED positional); a
differential rule that collapses when OUR value is invalid ("unknown site_id" answers
both a missing key and an unregistered one); 126 MUTATING calls replayed against ONE
shared world, so an apiDelete made every later verdict a function of replay ORDER; a
type-correct but MEANING-WRONG fixture (`text` for import/start is the operator's
pasted URL LIST, not prose); and a stub runner that invented attributes and produced
500s the product never had.

The guard that stops all five: a RESOURCE/VALUE complaint -- or an empty error message
-- can NEVER return DEAD. It returns FIXTURE-GAP, a named admission that our world is
too thin to judge that endpoint. A to-do list, not a verdict.

## v3.66.728 -- the /api/batch/* CONTROL cluster: retry, move, dedup_scan

Three of the 38 genuinely-dark CONTROL endpoints, all on one page. `BatchOps.tsx` already wired
`/api/batch/delete` with a dry-run PREVIEW then a typed-confirm live apply; the other three share
the same `{filter, dry_run}` contract and were reachable from nothing. They now reuse the SAME
filter, so what you previewed is what acts.

**THE DEAD-CONTROL TRAP, avoided on purpose.** `/api/batch/move` REQUIRES `target_dir` and answers
`400 "target_dir required"` without it. A move button posting `{filter, dry_run}` and no target
would be the exact 724 ("Delete ALL jobs") / 726 ("Start import") bug: the right route, a body the
endpoint refuses, and every ledger we own scoring it WIRED. It sends `target_dir`, the button is
disabled until one is set, and a test pins the endpoint's 400 so a bodyless mover can never become
silently "fine".

`dry_run` is sent EXPLICITLY on every call. The endpoints default it to True, and a control relying
on a default it cannot see is one refactor away from silently going live.

`dedup_scan` is a POST but is READ-ONLY -- it reports duplicates and changes nothing. It gets NO
confirm gate, deliberately, and a test pins that it does not grow one. A confirmation in front of a
call that mutates nothing is safety theatre, and theatre is how operators learn to click through
the real ones.

**THE 727 GATE PAID OFF IMMEDIATELY.** The type-aware body checker independently verified all four
batch controls as OK -- bodies actually ACCEPTED by the real endpoint, `move` included. It confirms
the controls WORK, not merely that a route literal appears in the source. That is the whole
difference between this and every ledger that scored two dead controls as wired.

Reachability: dark 119 -> 116. The sandbox caught the drift before stash did (the 725 ratchet check).

## v3.66.727 -- type-aware body checking: reading the 133 UNKNOWN

726's detector could only prove the sliver where a control passes a LITERAL `{}`. That sliver
alone held two dead controls. The other ~133 call sites pass the body as a TYPED VARIABLE --
`apiPost("/api/bulk/enqueue", req)` where `req: BulkEnqueueRequest` -- and a regex cannot see
into `req`.

The TYPE CHECKER can. `apiPost(path, payload: unknown)` declares nothing useful, but the
ARGUMENT EXPRESSION at each call site has an inferred type, and the compiler will hand it over.
`frontend/scripts/body_types.mjs` walks the TS program, asks the checker what each body IS,
and synthesizes a type-directed sample; `tools/body_contract.py` replays it against the real app.

SCOREBOARD (123 type-resolved call sites): 33 OK, 24 KEYS, 0 DEAD, 66 UNKNOWN.
Before this pass, every one of them was UNKNOWN.

  * DEAD    = the body type has NO KEYS and the endpoint refuses {}. The 724/726 shape, now
              provable for typed bodies. Pinned at 0.
  * KEYS    = a type-correct, NON-EMPTY key set. This CLOSES the empty-body class for that
              control -- it is not the 724/726 bug.
  * UNKNOWN = an open dict or unresolvable type. NOT A PASS.

WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT CLAIM. A 400 on a type-correct key set does NOT mean a dead
control. Our synthetic values ("x") are not real site ids, filenames or item ids, and a probe
CANNOT distinguish "missing key" from "invalid value" when the endpoint reports both
identically -- /api/queue/v2/cancel answers "unknown site_id" to BOTH. An earlier version of
this rule claimed otherwise and flagged 9 controls DEAD, including /api/tools/run, which we
WATCHED WORK LIVE at 719. Settling those needs REAL FIXTURES (a real site, a real draft file),
i.e. an integration harness -- not static or replay analysis. That limit is stated, not papered
over.

TWO FALSE POSITIVES THE BUILD ITSELF PRODUCED, both the same conflation, both fixed:
  * `Record<string, X>` has NO PROPERTIES, so the synthesizer emitted `flags: "x"` -- a STRING
    for an object param. The server rightly refused it and the probe blamed the CONTROL. It was
    the placeholder. (This is what flagged /api/tools/run.)
  * `Record<string, unknown>` at the TOP LEVEL is an OPEN DICT -- its keys are whatever the
    caller passes and are NOT statically knowable. Emitting `{}` for it made marketplace/import
    and its preview look like they send an empty body. "No keys" and "keys I cannot see" are
    DIFFERENT FACTS; collapsing them is the exact bug this whole line of work exists for. Open
    dicts are now UNKNOWN.

This is the sixth iteration of this detector. Every failed one failed identically: the
denominator did not contain the question.

## v3.66.726 -- the second dead control, the shadow route, and a gate so neither recurs

724 found a control that called the RIGHT endpoint with a body it REJECTS. Asking that
question properly turned up a SECOND one, and it had been shipping just as long.

**THE SECOND DEAD CONTROL.** `MoreActions.tsx` rendered a "Start import" button armed with
nothing but a site id, posting `{}` to `/api/import/start/<sid>`. That endpoint reads its
URLs from `{text: "url1\nurl2"}` or a file upload; with `{}` it resolves to `urls=[]` and
answers `400 "no valid URLs"`. EVERY TIME. There was no field anywhere on the page that
could have supplied the list -- a control cannot send what it never gathered. FIXED: the
Imports card now collects the URL list and sends `{text}`, and refuses to fire a request the
server will certainly refuse (a confirmation in front of a doomed call is theatre, not
safety).

**THE SHADOW.** `/api/sites/<sid>/bulk_reorder` REMOVED. It took `{order: [urls]}` and
duplicated `jobs/reorder` (`{ordering: {url: ord}}`), which SortableQueueGroup actually
calls. It was called by nothing but its own route. 724 nearly WIRED it -- which would have
added a second, worse path to the same behaviour and scored as a reachability WIN. A second
way to do one thing is not reachability, it is debt (the sched_exports precedent, 716).
`runner_queue.bulk_reorder()` stays: it is runner contract, pinned by test_v3_49_phase2, and
a separate blast radius.

**THE GATE.** `tools/body_contract.py` replays the body each control ACTUALLY SENDS against
the real app and reads the answer. DEAD is now pinned at 0. Every gate we owned scored both
dead controls as WIRED, because every one asked a question that could not see the bug:

    endpoint_reachability : "does a control reach this endpoint?"    -> yes
    bd-fe-dead-control    : "does this control reach anything?"      -> yes
    test_gui_parity       : "is the route literal in the FE source?" -> yes

Nobody asked DOES THE BODY SATISFY THE CONTRACT.

ON THE GATE'S HONESTY, which matters more than its coverage: it took FIVE attempts, and the
first four each reported confident nonsense -- 7, then 99, then 36 false positives -- for the
same reason every time: the denominator did not contain the question. It now claims DEAD only
for what it can PROVE (a literal `{}` sent to an endpoint that demands a body) and reports
the ~133 call sites it cannot judge as UNKNOWN (their bodies are typed variables a regex
cannot see into). UNKNOWN IS NOT A PASS. A gate that laundered those into OK would BE the bug
it exists to catch. Judging them needs type-aware analysis -- a real follow-on, not faked here.

Counts: 245 mutating call sites replayed -- 111 OK, 1 DEAD (now 0), 133 UNKNOWN.

Also: tests that grep for a route literal now STRIP COMMENTS first. Three times this session a
prose comment mentioning an endpoint satisfied -- or broke -- an assertion about a call to it.
A comment naming a route is not a control calling it.

## v3.66.725 -- re-pin the reachability ratchet (724 stash RED)

724 went RED on stash: `test_dark_ratchet_fell` -- dark=120, ledger pinned 127. The ratchet
working exactly as designed. Wiring 7 endpoints made 7 of them reachable (127 -> 120, an
IMPROVEMENT), and the gate demands the floor be re-pinned in the same cut so it cannot drift
back. Re-pinned: reports/endpoint_reachability.json dark_count 127 -> 120. The 7 that left
dark are precisely the 7 wired at 724; nothing became dark.

WHY THE SANDBOX MISSED IT -- two separate holes, both now closed:

1. THE BAND. I derived the band from the changed MODULES (Queue, SiteActions,
   app_sites_queue), and test_v3_66_719_tools_control.py names none of them. But 724 changed
   the gui_parity/reachability DENOMINATOR, and a denominator change has the blast radius of
   the DENOMINATOR, not the diff. Every ratchet over that denominator was in the band.

2. THE ENVIRONMENT -- and this one is the house bug again. Re-deriving the ledger under the
   sandbox runner (system python + PYTHONPATH=/tmp/prestaged_site_packages) gives dark=119,
   not 120, because httpx is absent there, so app_scrape_listing FAILS TO REGISTER, its route
   never enters url_map, and the endpoint VANISHES FROM THE DENOMINATOR -- counted "not dark"
   rather than "unknown". Pinning 119 would have gone RED on stash a second time. The
   reachability ledger must be built under the SERVICE VENV.

TOOLCHAIN (bdsuite rev-ax): bd-regen-order now CHECKS the reachability ratchet on every run
and re-pins only on --declare-reach. It runs that check under work/venv with PYTHONPATH
stripped, and if the venv is missing it SAYS it cannot verify and FAILS -- it does not fall
back to a python whose missing imports would silently shrink the denominator. Unknown is a
third state, and it fails. Negative controls run: a forged baseline is caught; a hidden venv
reports "CANNOT compute" rather than passing.

A ratchet nobody regenerates is a ratchet that only ever fires where it costs the most.

## v3.66.724 -- the site queue bulk-ops surface, and it ACTUALLY WORKS

The endpoint gap triage listed 12 CONTROL endpoints on `/api/sites/<sid>/`. Checked against
the source and the live app rather than trusted, the list was wrong in BOTH directions.

**A DEAD CONTROL, shipping.** `jobs/bulk_delete` was not missing a control -- it HAD one.
SiteActions rendered a bulk-delete button behind a typed hard-confirm, and its generic
`${suffix}` mutation posted `{}`. The endpoint requires `{urls: [...]}` and answers
`400 "urls must be a non-empty list"`. It failed 100% of the time, AFTER the operator typed
the confirmation. And the label lied twice: that endpoint has NO "all" semantic at any body
-- it deletes only the URLs you name. No request that button could send would do what it
said. A dead control is worse than a missing one: a missing one tells the truth; this one let
you believe the jobs were gone. REMOVED, and rebuilt where the URLs actually exist -- the
queue selection, which sends real urls and reports what the server actually removed.

**A SHADOW.** `bulk_reorder` (`{order: [urls]}`) duplicates `jobs/reorder`
(`{ordering: {url: ord}}`), which the SortableQueueGroup already uses. Called by nothing but
its own route. Deliberately NOT wired -- a second path to the same job is not reachability,
it is debt. Left visibly spa_wired=False; flagged for removal (the sched_exports precedent).

**FALSE POSITIVES.** `accounts/rotate` and `captcha/test` are wired and take no body, so `{}`
is correct for them. They read as CONTROL only because the parity scanner resolves ONE
interpolation, not two: `/api/sites/${siteId}/${suffix}` is invisible to it.

WIRED (6 new + 1 rebuilt), on the queue selection: `bulk_pause`, `bulk_resume`, `bulk_retry`,
`bulk_priority` (high/normal), `jobs/bulk_mark`, `jobs/bulk_priority`, `jobs/bulk_delete`
(confirm-gated). The selection spans SITES but every endpoint is PER-SITE, so the selection is
grouped by site and FANNED OUT; dispatching a cross-site selection at one sid would silently
drop every job on the other sites -- select 20, pause 7, get a success toast. Failures are
collected per site, so one bad site cannot hide the work that landed.

Call sites spell the route as a FULL literal, deliberately: wiring through a `${suffix}`
variable would fix the GUI and leave the ledger red forever -- see the false positives above.

**WHY THE LEDGER COULD NOT SEE ANY OF THIS:** its denominator is "route literals appearing in
frontend source". It cannot see a control wired through a template (false negative), and it
cannot see whether a wired control WORKS (a dead control reads as wired). It measures the
presence of a STRING, not the existence of a working CONTROL. Hence the tests here assert the
route path AND the request BODY -- body shape is exactly what the ledger is blind to, and
exactly what was broken.

spa_wired_total 387 -> 393 (+6; bulk_delete was already counted -- it moved, it was not added).

## v3.66.723 -- AF5: the automation safety nets become VISIBLE

Two guardrails shipped, worked, and reported to nobody.

- **706 restore rehearsal** -- the verdict IS persisted, and `backup_verify.last_rehearsal()`
  reads it back. That reader was called by NOTHING but its own test. A reader with no
  consumer is a verdict nobody hears.
- **708 pipeline halt** -- worse. `run_host_cycle` returns `{halted, halt_reason, errors}`,
  `scheduled_pipeline` passes it up, and the bg_scheduler task wrapper THREW THE RETURN
  VALUE AWAY. It was persisted nowhere. The comment above that code claimed the halt
  "surfaces on the AF5 timeline / AF7 digest". It surfaced on neither -- the comment
  ASSERTED the property instead of the code HAVING it.

Shipped:

- `automation_status.py` -- the read layer, plus the missing write. New `automation_cycles`
  table; `scheduled_pipeline` now PERSISTS every pass that ran (recorded there, not in the
  caller, so the verdict survives whoever drives the pass). A pass that did NOT run (toggle
  off, min-spacing) is deliberately NOT recorded: a no-op is not evidence of health.
- `app_automation_status.py` -- `GET /api/automation/status`. GET only; a readout is not a lever.
- `AutomationStatusPanel.tsx` -- both verdicts on screen, first thing in Settings ->
  Automation, above the switches. You should not arm what you cannot observe.

THE DESIGN RULE: **UNKNOWN IS A THIRD STATE, AND IT FAILS.** "I have never rehearsed" and
"I rehearsed and it passed" are different answers, and `ok` is False for the first. A
readout that infers "healthy" from "no failures found" is this codebase's dominant bug
shape -- a check whose denominator excludes the thing being asked about, reporting clean
truthfully and uselessly. On a fresh box the endpoint says `ok: false`, both nets `unknown`.
Silence is not consent.

Also fixed: `test_v3_66_711_automation_gui.py::test_automation_status_readouts_are_surfaced`
WAS A LIE and had been green for 12 releases. It asserted `"rehearsal" in src.lower()`,
which was satisfied by the TOGGLE labelled "Restore rehearsal" that 711 itself added -- so
it certified "readouts are surfaced" against a surface with no readout. It now DERIVES the
property: the frontend must call `/api/automation/status`, render the panel, and have an
UNKNOWN state.

## v3.66.721 -- three loose ends closed: a dropped gate, the vanishing venv, a lying number

#13 -- THE PK/WORK-TREE DIVERGENCE, RESOLVED BY EVIDENCE. Nine tools/*.py differed between the
project-knowledge bundle and the work tree. A function-level diff settles it: EIGHT are the work
tree being NEWER (it GAINED functions; PK is a stale snapshot). Exactly ONE lost something --
tasktracker_gen.py gained status() and DROPPED audit(), which no longer existed in the shipped
release. RESTORED, with its CLI flag and dispatch.

  Why it matters, in the function's own words: "--check only proves the md and xlsx agree with
  EACH OTHER (render drift). It passed IN-SYNC this release while a completed-section row carried
  the *incomplete* schema and rendered blank Version/State/Notes."

  That is the shape this entire session kept finding: A GATE THAT PASSES WHILE THE THING IT GUARDS
  IS BROKEN. --check compares two rendered artifacts to each other, so it is green whenever they
  agree -- including when they agree on garbage. --audit checks the DATA against its SCHEMA, which
  is the question actually being asked. RED-first; it caught both classes in the fixtures
  (a completed row with the incomplete schema; a duplicate ID across sections).

#14 -- THE VANISHING VENV, SOLVED. It did not vanish mysteriously. bd-install does
`rm -rf work/*` before extracting, and the release zip contains NO venv/ -- so re-running
bd-boot/bd-install mid-session DESTROYS the service venv and nothing restores it. This is a
SECOND consequence of FG-BOOT-REVERTS-WORKTREE that the footgun never stated (it only warned
about source edits being reverted). Every tool hardcoding venv/bin/python then silently probes
NOTHING -- which is exactly how bd-sbcap came to report "chromium build resolvable" having
verified nothing at all. FOOTGUNS.json now says so, with the fix (re-run bd-venv).

#15 -- A NUMBER THAT WAS STILL LYING. The route counts now reconcile exactly once units are
stated (bd-brief 1010 path x method / 970 paths == ROUTE_INDEX 1010 rows == url_map 970 unique
paths). But bd-parity-scan still reported "0 exec-bridged" AFTER the bridge shipped at 717,
because scan_bridges() asks only "does the backend subprocess into tools/*.py?" -- and
tool_bridge runs an ALLOWLISTED BINARY, not a tools/ script. Technically true; utterly
misleading. A reader concludes "no exec seam exists" -- the precise false premise the bridge was
built to fix. bd-parity-scan now states its unit AND reports the seam explicitly:

    tools: 215 total (tools/**/*.py, excl. _-prefixed) | 0 exec-bridged (tools/*.py)
    exec bridge: PRESENT (tool_bridge.py) -- 2 allowlisted binaries: ffprobe, yt-dlp

## v3.66.718 -- the 285 fail-closed test still named a deleted decoy

716's stash capture showed 4 failures. THREE were stale -- the capture ran a 716 tree whose
generated artifacts (DEPENDENCY_GRAPH.md, import_graph baseline) were regenerated in the 717
cut and are green there. ONE was a genuine miss my band did not catch:

test_v3_66_285_config_validation pins the validator's fail-CLOSED behaviour by writing a
config with a nested + bad-typed SAFETY key and asserting it loads to its safe default. Its
subject was `auto_refresh` -- one of the four decoys 716 DELETED. With the key gone from the
schema, the validator no longer treated it as safety-bearing, so the fail-closed assertion
failed. The behaviour under test is correct; the SUBJECT was deleted out from under it.

Re-pointed to the live successor automation.auto_refresh_enabled -- same fail-closed guarantee,
the key the runtime actually reads. Verified: every test that references a decoy literal is now
green (the rest use the short TOGGLE NAME via is_enabled(), which is unaffected -- the toggle
name maps to the dotted key, it is not the deleted schema key).

BAND LESSON: my consumer band derives from `grep module_name tests/`. test_v3_66_285 SETS the
schema key by literal without importing the inventory, so it was outside that grep. When a cut
DELETES A CONFIG KEY, the band must also be `grep "<key>" tests/` -- the consumers of a deleted
value are the tests that name it, not only the tests that import the module.

## v3.66.717 -- Cut 7: the exec bridge. The seam that did not exist.

tools_exec_bridged = 0: no code path took a GUI value and passed it as an argument to a tool.
That is the whole reason 739 CLI flags could not be exposed incrementally -- there was nothing
to hang a control on. Operator decision: build ONE validated, allowlisted bridge, built once
and built paranoid. All 739 become addressable through it.

bulk_downloader/tool_bridge.py + app_tool_bridge.py. The value is entirely in what it REFUSES;
the safe default is DENY:

- ALLOWLIST IS DATA. {tool: {argv0, flags:{name: spec}}}. A tool not in it cannot run; a flag
  not in its entry cannot be passed. Adding a capability is a diff to a reviewed dict, never a
  new code path. Starts read-only: yt-dlp + ffprobe (the download/probe engines), version /
  list-extractors / dump-json / -version only. yt-dlp's --exec is NOT allowlisted (on purpose).
- argv0 is a RESOLVED ABSOLUTE PATH captured at import from the allowlist. The request names a
  tool by KEY and never supplies a path -- proven: /bin/sh, ../../etc/passwd, "bash",
  "python3 -c" are all refused.
- NO SHELL. subprocess with a list argv, shell=False, _USES_SHELL pinned False by a test. A
  "; rm -rf /" payload in a flag value becomes ONE inert argv element -- proven live: it never
  reaches a shell, and validation usually refuses it before it becomes an argument at all.
- every value TYPE/RANGE validated: bool (token only), int (bounded), enum (fixed set), str
  (bounded, no control chars), path (realpath must resolve UNDER an allowed root -- traversal
  and absolute escape both refused, proven with ../../../../etc/passwd).
- hard TIMEOUT (30s) + output CAP (256 KiB/stream); a minimal env (PATH/HOME only, no inherited
  secrets); CSRF-gated like every mutating endpoint (enforced once a session exists).

Contract: RED-first, 11 tests, the negative controls ARE the spec -- unlisted tool, unlisted
flag, shell metacharacters, path traversal, CSRF, timeout/cap all pinned. 11/11 green. A real
`yt-dlp --version` call runs and returns bounded output.

Cut 8 lands the control surface that drives /api/tools/available + /api/tools/run. The endpoint
is live now so the listing is reachable; /api/tools/run is classified in the reachability ledger
until the control lands.

Route add (2) + new import edge: ROUTE_INDEX, route_map (re-frozen + SHA), ENDPOINT_CATALOG,
import_graph baseline all regenerated in-cut. FG-SPA-WIRING-ROUTE-INDEX (added rev-aq) guarded it.

## v3.66.716 -- remove the decoys and the shadow (two operator decisions, executed)

DECISION 1 -- the four non-dotted autonomy keys were DECOYS. Deleted.

  auto_promote / auto_quarantine / auto_refresh / auto_repair were DECLARED in
  GLOBAL_CONFIG_SCHEMA with safety=True, so a POST was accepted and PERSISTED. NOTHING read
  them. lifecycle_automation.is_enabled(name) maps the short toggle NAME through
  AUTOMATION_TOGGLES to the DOTTED key, and _read_toggle reads only that. An operator setting
  auto_refresh: true -- the obvious name, declared, safety-flagged, 200 OK, persisted -- got
  NOTHING. The feature stayed off.

  That is exactly the failure the comment DIRECTLY ABOVE the schema warns about: code reading
  get("auto_refresh") silently gets the default -- the feature is silently OFF (the 266
  footgun). The schema was carrying the footgun it was written to prevent.

  Thanks to the 709 write contract, a POST to them now 400s LOUDLY instead of lying with 200.
  Every automation consumer suite stays green -- proof that nothing read them.
  Open parity debt: 11 -> 7 (the decoys were 4 of the 11).

DECISION 2 -- /api/sched_exports was a SHADOW. Removed (app_sched_exports.py, 4 routes).

  Nothing called it. app_scheduled_exports is the family the SPA actually uses. The bare
  string "sched_exports" in useGovernance.ts is a react-query CACHE KEY, not a URL -- which
  fooled my prose AND my first reachability matcher into reporting the shadow as live (fixed
  at 715). bg_scheduler is untouched: it imports the LIBRARY (scheduled_exports), never the
  blueprint. Mutating endpoints 397 -> 394; dark 130 -> 127.

  route_map baseline RE-FROZEN (1000 -> 996 rules) and its SHA pin restated. The pin exists to
  make an ACCIDENTAL baseline edit impossible and it did its job: it blocked the cut until the
  change was declared intentional.

## v3.66.715 -- reachability matcher: a CACHE KEY is not a call site

A fourth false-positive class, found while answering the sched_exports question.

useGovernance.ts contains the string "sched_exports" -- as a react-query CACHE KEY
(`queryKey: ["sched_exports", "list"]`). It calls only /api/scheduled_exports/*. The 714
matcher tail-matched the bare identifier and certified /api/sched_exports and
/api/sched_exports/run_due as WIRED when nothing calls them. I made the same mistake in
prose before the tool did, and reported the family as live.

Path fragments carry a SLASH. Tail matching now requires a leading "/", so an identifier
that merely shares an endpoint's name cannot masquerade as a caller. Negative control added.

Dark: 119 -> 130. The 11 that surfaced were hidden behind name-collisions, not wired. The
ledger now classifies the three /api/sched_exports routes as SUPERSEDED: app_sched_exports.py
is shadowed by app_scheduled_exports.py, which is the family the SPA actually calls.
OPERATOR DECISION pending: remove the shadowed family.

130 dark = 26 dev-surface (gated by _dev_mode_guard) + 6 machine-to-machine + 3 superseded +
95 operator gaps.

## v3.66.714 -- A-GUI Cut 5: endpoint reachability. The VPN kill switch had no control.

A route existing is not reachability. A CONTROL that calls it is. 397 mutating endpoints;
119 are called by nothing -- no SPA component, no console, no extension. Reachable only by
someone who already knows they are there and hand-crafts a POST.

THE ONE THAT MATTERED: /api/vpn/system_killswitch/<id>/{plan,apply,commit,revert}. Vpn.tsx
already RENDERED this kill switch's state -- available / active rule sets / reason -- and
called NONE of its four endpoints. The GUI showed you the state of a kill switch it could
not operate. Same shape as automation.master_off_switch before 709/711: a safety control the
operator can see and cannot reach. Now wired: plan is a DRY RUN (computes the rule set,
changes nothing, no confirm); apply / commit / revert change system-level network state and
are confirm-gated, with copy that states the DIRECTION (revert REMOVES protection; a wrong
apply can cut connectivity to the host).

THE LEDGER (tools/endpoint_reachability.py + reports/endpoint_reachability.json). Every
mutating endpoint is WIRED or CLASSIFIED with a reason. Dark is allowed; dark and unexplained
is not. The dark count is a RATCHET -- it may only fall. 119: 24 dev-surface (gated by
_dev_mode_guard), 4 machine-to-machine (peer nodes / rate coordinator), 91 operator gaps
awaiting triage.

GETTING THE MATCHER RIGHT WAS THE WHOLE JOB. Three ways to be wrong, each found by a failing
negative control:
  * Matching the full rule string reported 117 dark. 40 were FALSE -- callers build URLs from
    fragments (`"/cockpit/api/shell/" + verb`) or template literals (`/api/sites/${id}/x`), so
    the rule never appears verbatim. A gate that cries wolf 40 times gets switched off.
  * Matching a parameterized rule's static STEM is worse: /api/sites/<sid>/purge has stem
    "/api/sites", so ONE apiPost to /api/sites would certify every /api/sites/... endpoint --
    including the dangerous ones -- as wired. Parameterized rules now require every static
    part: the prefix AND the suffix.
  * Blobbing all of tools/ as a "console" caller certified the kill switch as WIRED, because a
    CLI script posts to it. A CLI caller is not an operator surface. That is exactly the
    mistake this ledger exists to stop -- confusing "something calls it" with "an operator can
    reach it" -- and it hid the one finding that mattered. Consoles are now the four
    server-rendered console modules, named.

The FE spells the kill-switch endpoint out PER VERB instead of interpolating `.../${verb}`: a
templated verb is invisible to any static scan, so the ledger could not prove the control
reached commit/revert. A control whose target is not legible is one nobody can audit.

Frontend: tsc clean; 424 tests green.

## v3.66.713 -- A-GUI Cut 4: the layers the inventory never knew existed

710 fixed the denominator for the layers the inventory KNEW about. These are the ones it
did not know were there. Config surface 447 -> 475, and open debt stays at 11: scanning a
surface must TRACK it, not manufacture debt no control could ever close.

- ENV BEYOND .py. The env-tranche gate scans .py only, so 12 deploy/install knobs living in
  shell scripts were invisible to the gate whose entire job is making prefixed literals
  impossible to miss. Scanned now, classified deploy-only (display-only): the process is
  already running by the time a GUI could write them.
- ENV BEYOND THE PREFIX. The scan matches the project prefix, so 5 unprefixed runtime vars
  were unscored -- including CLOAKBROWSER_BINARY_PATH, which selects the browser BINARY that
  gets EXECUTED during capture. test_gui_parity asserted `all(key.startswith("BD_"))`: that
  assertion did not describe reality, it CREATED the blind spot -- the scan matched the
  prefix, so an unprefixed var could not be seen, and the test then certified that none
  existed. (And the NETNS_* vars are deliberately unprefixed to DODGE
  FG-ENV-TRANCHE-BD-LITERAL, so the gate's own pressure keeps producing surface it cannot
  see.)
- DB-BACKED CONFIG (4) -- capture_schedules / scheduled_exports / api_auth_tokens /
  share_tokens. Config that lives in SQLite rather than a file or an env var. A GUI control
  exists for each; nothing had ever counted them.
- PLUGIN MANIFEST fields (8) -- scored 0 before.
- PERSISTED STORES (11) recorded. _scan_other_stores was a hand-list of exactly TWO modules.
  Recorded as STORES, not as parity rows: app_config.json BACKS global_config, so counting it
  as a setting would double-count every key inside it.
- ENV LOCKS are an ATTRIBUTE, not rows. app.py's _origins_env_locked does
  os.environ.get(prefix + field.upper()), so every global_config key has an implicit env
  override. All 90 are overrides of settings ALREADY COUNTED. Recording them as rows would
  double-count the store. A denominator padded with duplicates is no more honest than one
  that truncates.

FG-ENV-TRANCHE-BD-LITERAL bit this cut WHILE WRITING IT: the new scanner's own COMMENTS named
two deploy vars literally, _scan_env scans that file too, and the inventory invented two
phantom env vars with runtime_tunable=True -- which showed up as fake open debt. The footgun
is real and it does not care that you are the one documenting it. Literals scrubbed.

Also fixed: de-dup keyed on (KIND, key), never on key alone. A per-site key and a
global_config key can share a NAME while being different settings in different scopes;
deduping on name silently dropped a global_config key (90 -> 89).

## v3.66.710 -- A-GUI Cut 2: the DENOMINATOR (why every gate read clean)

Three gates reported healthy while the emergency stop was dead. None of them lied; each
asserted over a denominator that excluded the thing being asked about.

- CFG_FIELDS was read with a NON-GREEDY regex -- `CFG_FIELDS\s*=\s*\[(.*?)\]` -- which
  truncates at the first nested ']'. It returned 39 of 235 keys, so the config inventory
  scored 57 per-site keys and every parity number was a fraction of the wrong denominator.
  Parsed with AST now: a list is a list, not a substring.
  The truncation was KNOWN: app_settings_center._gated_editor_field_set() deliberately
  MIRRORED it, reasoning that it "deliberately excludes structured fields like accounts".
  But a truncation is not an allowlist -- to withhold ONE credential field it also dropped
  ~180 unrelated keys. `accounts` (nested per-account credentials) is now withheld
  EXPLICITLY via _STRUCTURED_CREDENTIAL_FIELDS. Same protection, stated instead of accidental.
- The GUI manifest collapsed the ENTIRE global_config store into one row,
  "(global_config store)": "full" -- 90 keys behind a single assertion. The ratchet counts
  ROWS, so it read open=0 while automation.master_off_switch was unwritable. Enumerated per
  key now; the excuse in the code ("keys are not statically enumerable in source") was false --
  GLOBAL_CONFIG_SCHEMA declares every one.
- gui_exposure is DERIVED, not ASSERTED. The inventory used to hardcode every site key to
  "partial" and let a hand-maintained manifest override it -- i.e. it asserted GUI exposure
  with ZERO knowledge of what the GUI renders. Exposure now comes from the thing that builds
  the form (app_settings_center._editable_field_set / _gated_editor_field_set, the descriptor
  SiteSettings.tsx actually renders).

RESULT -- the denominator: 178 -> 447 items. site_key 57 -> 237. global_config 1 row -> 90 keys.
Per-site GUI coverage is 234 of 235 (only `accounts`, by design) -- so per-site parity was
always BETTER than the inventory claimed. The inventory's errors ran in BOTH directions, which
is worse than a wrong number: it was a number nobody could sign.

RATCHET BASELINE 0 -> 37, re-pinned COLD (BDTOOLS_CACHE=0). The 0 was never real. The 37 is:
the 26 automation.* keys declared at 709 plus the legacy autonomy globals (auto_promote,
auto_quarantine, auto_refresh, auto_repair, ...) that have no GUI control. Cut 3 lands those
controls and the number falls. `accounts` is NOT counted as debt -- _NEVER_EXPOSE marks it a
decided exclusion, not undelivered parity.

The A-GUI gap is now a NUMBER (26 automation keys at gui_exposure=none) instead of a blind spot.

Tests amended, not weakened: three 310 invariants ("every site key is full") held only because
`accounts` was invisible; they now STATE the exclusion. test_parity_baseline_stays_at_zero_open
pinned a floor of 0 that was an artifact of not looking; it now pins the ratchet PROPERTY
(open == baseline, may only fall).

## v3.66.709 -- A-GUI Cut 1: the global_config WRITE CONTRACT (the no-op-write class)

The emergency stop could not be turned on. POST /api/global_config
{"automation.master_off_switch": true} returned 200 OK and wrote NOTHING: the generic write
path iterates GLOBAL_CONFIG_SCHEMA and skips anything absent, and 21 automation keys the
runtime READS were never DECLARED there. The endpoint's own comment describes the bug it was
built to fix ("the 306 latent bug where schema keys with no explicit branch were silently
dropped (POST 200, nothing written)") -- and the same bug survived, in the one place it
mattered most.

- CONTRACT FIRST. An unrecognised key is now 400, not accepted-and-discarded. Declaring the
  missing keys alone would have left the next undeclared key to recreate this just as
  silently. A discarded write reporting SUCCESS is precisely why every parity gate read clean
  while the kill switch was dead.
- 21 automation.* keys DECLARED (automation.* in the schema: 5 -> 26). master_off_switch is
  safety-bearing with safe_default=True -- the only key whose fail-closed value is True,
  because a malformed config must STOP autonomy, never leave it running. Download-affecting
  L4/L5 toggles fail closed to DISABLED; scrub_on_capture_enabled (redaction, ships ON) fails
  closed to ON.
- _EXPLICIT_BRANCH_KEYS is PINNED TO SOURCE by a test rather than hand-maintained: a stale
  hand-list is the exact drift class this cut exists to kill. Add an explicit branch without
  updating the set and the build fails, instead of 400ing a legitimate write in production.
- Self-maintaining gate: every automation key the runtime reads must be declared. Add a reader
  without a declaration and the build fails.

RED-first: 19/20 failed on pristine source (the lone pass was the negative control). Now 21/21.
Banded across 17 suites (~230 tests): global_config family, settings UI, security, contracts,
rate-limit, the env-tranche/parity count-pin family, site-editor parity, and the full
automation family (706/707/708, lifecycle, controller).

NOTE: the keys are now writable via the API. There is still NO GUI control for them -- that is
Cut 3. Until then the off-switch is reachable by API only.

## v3.66.708 -- A-PIPE / A9: the capstone. The automation program is now CONNECTED.

THE FINDING that shaped this cut: the automation program was ~90% BUILT and 0% RUNNING.
A0 (gold backup, @471), A1 (lifecycle.drift_sweep, registered), A2/A5 (keystone-backed
refresh via lifecycle_drift.on_fresh_capture), A3 (the quarantined state machine),
A-REPAIR (drift_repair.daily -> review-only drafts), X-AUTO-1 (@706) and X-AUTO-2 (@707)
ALL EXIST -- and `automation_controller.run_host_cycle`, the ONE function that executes an
autonomous cycle (off-switch, trust gates, audit trail, ceiling), was called by NOTHING.
No scheduler task. No route. The engine was built and never connected to anything -- the
same "built but never wired" shape as bd-brief, the @extractor registry (dead until 691)
and smoke_restore (dead until 706).

NEW `bulk_downloader/automation_pipeline.py` -- the ordered, checkpointed chain:
    capture -> build -> lint -> blocked_scan -> drift_stage -> apply
run as ONE flow with a rollback point at each stage, through run_host_cycle.

SAFETY PROPERTIES, each pinned by a test:
  * ORDER IS SAFETY -- lint and blocked_scan MUST precede drift_stage/apply, or the
    pipeline could apply a template it never checked.
  * A FAILED STAGE HALTS THE CHAIN. Deliberately the OPPOSITE of run_host_cycle's step
    behaviour ("a throwing step is isolated, the loop continues"): steps in a cycle are
    INDEPENDENT; stages in a pipeline are SEQUENTIAL AND DEPENDENT. Carrying on past a
    failed lint would apply a template that failed its check -- the failure would compound
    instead of stopping. Proven: when lint throws, `apply` NEVER runs.
  * MUTATING STAGES (drift_stage, apply) ARE A0-BACKED and FAIL-CLOSED: a restorable
    snapshot is taken first (delegating to template_backup, never re-derived), and if it
    CANNOT be taken the stage does NOT run. An autonomous overwrite without a recovery
    point is exactly what A0 exists to forbid.
  * IT RUNS THROUGH run_host_cycle -- the off-switch, trust gates, audit trail and the
    707 ceiling are INHERITED, not re-implemented. Two budgets would be two behaviours.
  * DEFAULT OFF (automation.pipeline_enabled). Registering the bg task is
    behaviour-neutral.

Stage bodies are inert placeholders by default: this module owns the ORDER and the
CHECKPOINTS, and injects the real step implementations -- so the capstone never silently
re-implements a step that already exists elsewhere in the program.

OPERATOR NOTE (in the config comment too): turn pipeline_enabled ON only AFTER exercising
the parts -- the 706 restore rehearsal proving the backups restore, and the 707 ceiling
proving a failing loop halts. That sequence IS the "proven full reversibility" A-PIPE is
gated on. It is not a formality.

RED-first: 9 tests. NON-guard, no route.

## v3.66.707 -- X-AUTO-2: a CEILING on the autonomous cycle

`automation_controller.run_host_cycle` is the ONE place autonomous action happens, and
its only brake was the MASTER OFF-SWITCH -- which is binary, all-or-nothing. Past that
gate, the loop ran EVERY injected step with no wall-clock limit, no step cap, and -- the
runaway -- it CONTINUED AFTER A FAILURE. Its own docstring said so: "a throwing step is
isolated + audited, the loop continues". A pipeline failing every step kept right on
executing steps: a broken autonomous loop, burning actions, not knowing it was broken.

A-PIPE (the capstone multi-stage pipeline) does not exist yet, so a literal "per-stage"
ceiling has nothing to attach to. The guardrail the plan actually wants does: a per-CYCLE
ceiling on the loop autonomy runs TODAY.

NEW `automation_controller.AutoBudget` (max_steps / wall_s / max_errors), deliberately
the same idiom as run_budget.RunBudget -- one budget shape across the codebase. Checked
BEFORE each step, so a breach prevents the NEXT action rather than merely noticing the
last one. A ceiling is a HALT, not a skip: on breach the cycle STOPS and records WHY. A
guardrail that lets the loop finish "just this once" is not a guardrail. The halt is
surfaced in the result (halted / halt_reason / errors) -- a guardrail the operator cannot
see fired is not a guardrail.

Config: automation.cycle_max_steps / cycle_wall_s / cycle_max_errors, all DEFAULT 0 =
UNCAPPED, so an unconfigured cycle is BYTE-IDENTICAL to pre-707 (pinned by a NEG control,
including "a throwing step is isolated and the loop continues"). An operator running L2
autonomy should set cycle_max_errors.

ORDERING PINNED: the master off-switch still DOMINATES a permissive budget -- a master
stop must never be reachable-past.

RED-first: 9 tests, 9 RED on pristine 706. NON-guard, no route.

HARNESS NOTE (caught pre-stash): the arming fixture was written as @pytest.fixture
(autouse=True) taking `monkeypatch`. run_tests.py -- the harness capture.sh actually runs
-- does NOT inject monkeypatch into an AUTOUSE fixture (it does for a test's own args),
so the gates were never patched and 6 tests silently failed under the real harness while
pytest reported 9/9 green. Converted to an explicit _arm(monkeypatch) call. Same class as
the 704 xfail catch: PYTEST-GREEN IS NOT HARNESS-GREEN, and the harness is the authority.

## v3.66.706 -- X-AUTO-1: restore REHEARSAL (first cut of the A0-unblocked track)

A0 (the keystone) was DECLARED LANDED this session -- it turned out to have SHIPPED at
v3.66.471 and simply never been declared, which is why the whole automation track stayed
blocked. A0 guarantees a backup is TAKEN and RESTORABLE AT WRITE TIME
(template_keystone.safe_overwrite ABORTS the write if the generational backup cannot be
taken; proven by test_safe_overwrite_aborts_when_backup_fails).

This cut adds the other half. `backup_verify.smoke_restore()` -- the function that PROVES
a backup on disk still restores -- was reachable ONLY from a manual API call
(POST /api/backup/smoke_restore). NOTHING ever ran it. So nobody had ever confirmed the
backups sitting on disk still restore. backup_verify's own docstring has always said it:
"A backup that's never restored is a wish, not a backup ... Designed to run nightly via
bg_scheduler" -- and it never was.

NEW `backup_verify.rehearse()`: find the latest backup, smoke_restore it into a temp
sandbox, persist the verdict. Fail-soft (never raises into the scheduler). NOT-ok is the
honest answer for an unrestorable archive AND for NO BACKUP AT ALL -- "no backup on disk"
is not "fine", it is the loudest possible failure of a backup system and must never read
as ok. The rehearsal restores into a sandbox and NEVER touches live: a verification that
mutates what it verifies is not a verification.

THE LOAD-BEARING RULE: the daily digest is ZERO-DELTA-SILENT (a quiet day sends nothing,
to protect the operator's inbox). A FAILED REHEARSAL BREAKS THAT SILENCE. A broken backup
on a quiet day is exactly what must NOT be silent -- silence would read as "all fine"
while the recovery path you depend on is broken. A PASSING rehearsal does NOT break it:
the escape hatch stays narrow, or the digest would fire daily, get muted, and defeat its
own purpose. Both directions are pinned by tests.

Wired into the existing scheduled_digest pass. Opt-in, DEFAULT OFF
(`automation.restore_rehearsal_enabled`, a GLOBAL key -> no settings-center count-pin
coupling). Inert until the operator turns it on: with no rehearsal supplied the digest
body and behaviour are byte-identical to pre-706 (pinned by a NEG control).

RATCHET INCIDENT (found by this cut, fixed here): the gate BLOCKED on defect_DP_total
2205 -> 2207, but the +2 was NOT from this cut. Cold-scanning EVERY shipped release with
the cache disabled proved it: 701, 702, 703, 704 and 705 ALL measure 2207. The baseline
of 2205 NEVER matched a single shipped tree -- it was inherited from a previous session's
bd_metrics_baseline.json and restored at session start without ever being validated.
Worse: the gate PASSED three cuts (703/704/705) reading 2205, because bd-defect-scan is
memoized and a STALE CACHE HIT served the wrong total to the ratchet. The truth only
surfaced when capture_bodies changed at 705 and forced a cache miss.
  ROOT LESSON: A GATE MUST NEVER TRUST A CACHE. A stale hit is a silent false-GREEN --
  exactly the class the cache's content-hash keying was meant to prevent (and the keying
  IS sound: cache ON == OFF == 2207 today). The bug was USING it at a gate at all.
  FIX: bd-ratchet now forces BDTOOLS_CACHE=0 -- the ratchet measures COLD, every time.
  The cache stays (17.9s -> 0.11s) for human/interactive use. Baseline re-pinned to the
  cold-verified 2207 -- not to unblock this cut, but because 2205 was never real.
  The 2 findings are pre-existing DP-09s in capture_bodies (_redact_json / redact_body
  branch on dict/list/str but not bytes/set) -- untouched by any cut this session.

RED-first: 10 tests, 9 RED on pristine 705. Controls include "an UNRESTORABLE backup is
DETECTED" (a rehearsal that cannot fail proves nothing) and both silence directions.
End-to-end verified: a corrupt backup on a quiet day fires
"BulkDownloader: RESTORE REHEARSAL FAILED". NON-guard: 7 guards byte-identical. No route.

## v3.66.705 -- GUARD CUT: close the capture-time floor's ATTRIBUTE-PREFIX leak

GUARD CHANGE DECLARED: bulk_downloader/capture_bodies.py 2d851646 -> 6c7f5c9a.
The other 6 release guards are byte-identical. Single-concern guard cut.

THE BUG (found by the 704 coverage cut, which pinned it with a characterization test):
`_TOKENISH` is r"\S+", so a token carried by an ATTRIBUTE is ONE whitespace-bounded
token -- `data-token="eyJhbGci..."` -- and BOTH the leading `data-token="` prefix AND the
trailing markup (`">x</a>`) rode along with it. `_value_is_dangerous`'s patterns are
ANCHORED (^eyJ... / ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{32,}), so they never matched, and the secret was stored
RAW. Any token behind a `key="` prefix slipped through: HTML data-attrs, `src=`/`href=`,
and an unparseable-JSON body's `"token":"..."` (which falls through to this text scrub).
This contradicted the scrub's OWN comment, which names "an HTML data-attr" as the very
case it exists to catch.

SEVERITY: NOT an egress leak. The SHARE-time scrubber (tools/capture_scrub.scrub_string)
already masked this shape -- verified -- so the .redacted.wacz twin that actually gets
shared was always clean. The hole was in the capture-time FLOOR: the raw local capture
stored a live credential despite the comment's "so we cannot store it raw".

THE FIX: the value CARRIED BY the attribute is now tested too, in both forms -- quoted
(`data-token="eyJ..."`, `"token":"eyJ..."`) and bare (`session=<tok>`). Only the dangerous
VALUE is replaced, so the attribute name and the surrounding markup SURVIVE
(`<a data-token="<scrubbed>">x</a>`) -- the capture exists to preserve that structure.

OVER-REDACTION NEG CONTROLS (the risk of any widened scrub): a scrub that masks everything
destroys the DOM/playlist the capture is storing. Pinned: `width=1280 height=720
charset=utf-8`, `<a href="/about/contact">`, and HLS directives
(`#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=1280x720`) all survive BYTE-IDENTICAL.

RED-first: 11 tests, 3 RED on pristine 704 (the leak), 5 neg controls green before AND
after (they pin what must not change). The 704 characterization test INVERTED -- it failed
as "unexpectedly fixed" the moment the guard landed and forced itself to be flipped,
exactly as designed. The finding could not be silently forgotten.
